body:
Childhood & Early Life

Robert Burns was born on 25 January 1759 in Alloway, Ayrshire, in a clay cottage his father William had built with his own hands. William was a tenant farmer who scraped at poor land and still insisted his sons learn to read, so he hired a young teacher, John Murdoch, to share the lessons among the neighbours' children. Robert grew up on the Bible, Scottish ballads and the songs and stories of an old woman in the household, Betty Davidson, who knew every ghost and fairy tale in Ayrshire.

The farming was brutal. By his teens Robert was doing a man's work in the fields, and he later said the labour left him stooped and with a weak heart and a nervous, sleepless body. He wrote his first song at fifteen, for a girl called Nelly Kilpatrick who worked beside him at the harvest.

What He Did & Why He's Remembered

Burns wrote in the Scots his neighbours spoke, at a time when polite Scotland was embarrassed by it, and made it sound like the language of kings and lovers. He also collected and rewrote hundreds of folk songs for the Scots Musical Museum, often refusing payment, so that tunes that might have died were kept. "Auld Lang Syne," "A Red, Red Rose" and "To a Mouse" are still sung and quoted around the world. Scots celebrate his birthday every year with a Burns Supper, which is a little absurd for a poor farmer, and also a little perfect.

Family Life

His father died in 1784, broken by debt and a lawsuit with a landlord, when Robert was twenty-five. Robert and his brother Gilbert tried to keep the farm at Mossgiel going. Burns had at least a dozen children by several women, some outside marriage, and the kirk made him sit in public rebuke on the stool of repentance for it. He supported them all in the end, including the illegitimate ones, as best he could.

Romantic Life

Love was the engine of most of his best writing, and the cause of most of his trouble. Jean Armour became pregnant by him in 1786, and her father had the marriage papers torn up. Burns, humiliated and broke, booked passage to Jamaica to work on a plantation, and published his poems to pay for the ticket. The book, the Kilmarnock edition, sold so well that he stayed, and it made him famous at twenty-seven.

In Edinburgh he was the ploughman poet, the toast of the salons, and he fell for Agnes Maclehose, a deserted wife who wrote to him as "Clarinda" while he signed himself "Sylvander." When she sailed to join her husband in the West Indies in 1791, he wrote "Ae Fond Kiss," which Walter Scott thought held the essence of a thousand love poems. He did marry Jean Armour in 1788, and she raised his children, including those from other women, with a patience that is hard to fully understand.

Life Until Death

Burns took a farm at Ellisland, failed at it, and became an excise officer in Dumfries, riding hundreds of miles a week collecting duty on whisky. He kept writing songs for George Thomson's collection, mostly for free. His health collapsed from rheumatic fever and a damaged heart; the legend that drink killed him is mostly myth. He died on 21 July 1796, aged thirty-seven, the day his youngest son was born. Thousands attended the funeral in Dumfries. Jean was left with five children and no money, and admirers raised a fund for her.

His Works

A Red, Red Rose (1794)

O my Luve's like a red, red rose
That's newly sprung in June;
O my Luve's like the melodie
That's sweetly play'd in tune.

As fair art thou, my bonnie lass,
So deep in luve am I;
And I will luve thee still, my dear,
Till a' the seas gang dry.

Till a' the seas gang dry, my dear,
And the rocks melt wi' the sun;
And I will luve thee still, my dear,
While the sands o' life shall run.

And fare thee weel, my only Luve!
And fare thee weel awhile!
And I will come again, my Luve,
Tho' it were ten thousand mile.

Ae Fond Kiss (1791)

Ae fond kiss, and then we sever;
Ae fareweel, alas, for ever!
Deep in heart-wrung tears I'll pledge thee,
Warring sighs and groans I'll wage thee.

Who shall say that Fortune grieves him,
While the star of hope she leaves him?
Me, nae cheerfu' twinkle lights me;
Dark despair around benights me.

I'll ne'er blame my partial fancy,
Naething could resist my Nancy;
But to see her was to love her,
Love but her, and love for ever.

Had we never lov'd sae kindly,
Had we never lov'd sae blindly,
Never met—or never parted,
We had ne'er been broken-hearted.

Fare-thee-weel, thou first and fairest!
Fare-thee-weel, thou best and dearest!
Thine be ilka joy and treasure,
Peace, Enjoyment, Love and Pleasure!

Ae fond kiss, and then we sever;
Ae fareweel, alas, for ever!
Deep in heart-wrung tears I'll pledge thee,
Warring sighs and groans I'll wage thee.

To a Mouse, on turning her up in her nest with the plough, November 1785 (selected stanzas)

Wee, sleekit, cow'rin, tim'rous beastie,
O, what a panic's in thy breastie!
Thou need na start awa sae hasty,
Wi' bickering brattle!
I wad be laith to rin an' chase thee,
Wi' murd'ring pattle!

I'm truly sorry Man's dominion
Has broken Nature's social union,
An' justifies that ill opinion,
Which makes thee startle,
At me, thy poor, earth-born companion,
An' fellow-mortal!

But Mousie, thou art no thy lane,
In proving foresight may be vain:
The best-laid schemes o' Mice an' Men
Gang aft agley,
An' lea'e us nought but grief an' pain,
For promis'd joy!

Still thou art blest, compar'd wi' me!
The present only toucheth thee:
But Och! I backward cast my e'e,
On prospects drear!
An' forward, tho' I canna see,
I guess an' fear!

Auld Lang Syne (1788, first verse and chorus lines)

Should auld acquaintance be forgot,
And never brought to mind?
Should auld acquaintance be forgot,
And auld lang syne?

For auld lang syne, my dear,
For auld lang syne,
We'll tak a cup o' kindness yet,
For auld lang syne.

And there's a hand my trusty fiere,
And gie's a hand o' thine,
And we'll tak a right gude-willie waught,
For auld lang syne.

"The best-laid schemes o' Mice an' Men / Gang aft agley."
